Date: 26-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20127470
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: IT Category Manager
Purpose: ServiceNow’s Integrated AI Platform Pricing
Question Asked: Can Gartner help identify best practices and market insights regarding ServiceNow’s transition from modular pricing to an integrated AI platform commercial model? We are concerned about maintaining flexibility and cost transparency as ServiceNow moves away from its traditional modular approach. Specifically, we would like to understand how other enterprises are managing this shift, what strategies are being used to negotiate favorable terms, and what potential pitfalls to avoid. Additionally, does Gartner have any supportive market research or recommendations, such as those found in the Vendor Insight Report: ServiceNow, that can guide us in evaluating this new model and ensuring alignment with our procurement and IT cost optimization objectives?
Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: 🧠 Key Discussion Points
1) Shift to AI-based (token/credit) pricing model
The core focus of the discussion was ServiceNow’s transition from traditional SaaS licensing to AI consumption-based models (tokens/credits).
	• Historically:
		○ Customers purchased licences (e.g. ITSM, ITOM) per user/fulfiller.
		○ AI was optional via “Plus” add-ons, purchased separately and selectively.
	• New model:
		○ AI is embedded directly into base packages (e.g. ITSM Prime).
		○ Customers automatically receive token allocations tied to user licences.
		○ Tokens are required for every AI-driven action (e.g. workflows, responses, automation tasks).
Why this matters:
This fundamentally changes the cost structure from predictable SaaS spend to variable consumption-based spend, introducing significant uncertainty in budgeting and optimisation.
2) Structural inefficiencies in the new model
A major theme was the lack of flexibility and efficiency in how tokens are allocated:
	• Tokens are: 
		○ Purchased per user, per product
		○ Aggregated into a shared bucket within that product only
	• Tokens cannot be shared across products (e.g. ITSM vs HRSD).
	• Organisations may be forced to overbuy tokens: 
		○ Example: buying AI capacity for all users even if only a subset uses it.
Conclusion reached:
The current model risks systematic over-procurement and stranded capacity, especially in early AI adoption phases.
3) Uncertainty in forecasting and governance challenges
There was a clear acknowledgement that:
	• Customers cannot reliably forecast token usage upfront
	• Most organisations will: 
		○ Start with an estimate
		○ Then adjust (true-up) mid-contract
Two key risks were identified:
	1. Token overconsumption (“blowouts”)
	2. Lack of visibility into AI usage patterns
Why this matters:
Without strong governance, organisations risk significant unplanned cost escalation.
4) Overage and expansion cost risks
Two mechanisms for handling excess consumption were discussed:
	• Additional token packs
		○ Provide incremental capacity
		○ Once purchased, they are typically committed for the remainder of the contract
	• Overage pricing
		○ Pay-per-token beyond allocation
		○ Significantly higher unit cost
Conclusion reached:
Both options create risk:
	• Packs → long-term overcommitment
	• Overage → short-term cost spikes
5) Vendor control over token rate card
A major concern raised:
	• ServiceNow can change token consumption rates (rate card) over time
	• Example: an action costing 5 tokens today could cost more later
Why this matters:
This creates pricing volatility independent of usage, making it difficult to:
	• Predict costs
	• Protect commercial terms over time
6) Market maturity and expected evolution
Both parties aligned that:
	• The current model feels early-stage / immature
	• Likely future evolution: 
		○ More flexible token pooling
		○ Simplified pricing constructs
		○ Potential movement towards broader consumption bundles
Conclusion:
The model is not expected to remain in its current form long-term, especially by the client’s renewal timeline (2029).
📅 Action Items
Action	Owner	Due Date
Download and retain current ServiceNow AI token rate card for reference and benchmarking	Client (Fiorella)	Short term
Begin internal discussions on AI governance model (usage tracking, controls, approvals)	Client	Short term
Assess current ServiceNow footprint (ITSM, HRSD, etc.) to understand future token exposure	Client	Mid term
Provide internal alignment on procurement AI commercial frameworks (cross-vendor)	Client	Mid term
Share supporting ServiceNow documentation and artefacts	Domenico	Completed (during call)

Our current order form, which outlines the products, licensing and pricing for what we currently have in place and are seeking to renew.
Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: 🧠 Key Discussion Points & Conclusions
(from the meeting transcript)
1) Current ServiceNow position is strong for multi‑year renewal
	• The client’s current deal (~$177k/year for ~60–65 seats) includes a 5% price cap, which is materially better than typical market renewals.
	• Market norms discussed: 
		○ Typical 3-year renewals ≈ ~20% uplift
		○ Client is seeing ~5% uplift → materially favourable
	• Benchmark comparison: 
		○ Client’s per-seat pricing sits below Gartner benchmarks for CSM Pro
	• Conclusion:
→ The existing 3-year renewal option is objectively a strong, defensible deal based on benchmarks.
2) One-year option introduces pricing and leverage risk
	• Vendor initially resisted offering 1-year terms (despite this not being standard practice), then provided a non-standard 1-year offer (~$215k, ~15% uplift).
	• Observations: 
		○ Pricing sits outside benchmark ranges
		○ Premium vs 3-year is higher than expected (~>10%)
	• Critical commercial risks highlighted: 
		○ ServiceNow anchors future pricing on latest unit rate
		○ Moving to 1-year likely resets baseline at a higher level
		○ Future negotiations unlikely to reduce pricing (vendor historically does not reverse pricing)
	• Conclusion:
→ One-year option is strategically useful for flexibility, but commercially weak and likely to increase long-term costs.
3) Limited negotiation leverage at current spend level
	• Key insight: 
		○ ServiceNow prioritises deals ~$1M+ for meaningful concessions
		○ At ~$200k/year, the client is treated as SMB / low-leverage
	• Implication: 
		○ Threatening to leave may not materially influence pricing
		○ ServiceNow is relatively indifferent to losing smaller deals
	• Conclusion:
→ Negotiation leverage is structurally limited, so strategy must rely on positioning (alternatives, timing), not pressure.
4) Product fit concerns driving desire for flexibility
	• Client concerns: 
		○ High operational complexity
		○ Significant internal staffing required
		○ Limited self-service capability compared to alternatives (e.g., Zendesk)
	• Current usage: 
		○ Primarily internal help desk for ~1300-person organisation
	• Question raised: 
		○ Whether ServiceNow is over-engineered for current needs
	• Conclusion:
→ The 1-year option is being considered primarily for strategic evaluation of alternatives, not pricing optimisation.
5) Switching vs staying – key trade-off
	• Staying: 
		○ Strong pricing baseline
		○ Known platform
		○ Avoids transition cost and disruption
	• Switching: 
		○ Potentially better fit (simpler tools like Zendesk)
		○ Requires: 
			§ Migration effort
			§ Change management
			§ Rebuilding processes
	• Insight: 
		○ Competitors (Zendesk, Halo) are more motivated to discount to win business
	• Conclusion:
→ Decision should prioritise functional fit and total cost of ownership, not just licence price.
📅 Action Items
Action	Owner	Due Date
Evaluate whether ServiceNow remains the right platform for size and use case	Client	Within next ~2 months (pre-renewal decision window stated in meeting)
Engage alternative vendors (e.g., Zendesk, Halo ITSM) for comparison	Client	Urgent (not yet initiated; renewal is imminent)
Attempt to negotiate improvements on 3-year offer (positioning willingness to explore alternatives)	Client	Before renewal deadline (end of current month)

Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: 🧠 Detailed Key Discussion Points
1. E7 is predictable; token-based AI consumption is the bigger financial risk
The discussion opened with the client wanting to understand the implications of Microsoft 365 E7, especially how it could affect future cost modeling and capital committee decisions. The key point made was that E7 itself is not likely to be the biggest cost problem over the next five years. E7 was positioned as a relatively predictable SaaS-style cost, similar in nature to E5, because it bundles known products such as E5, Copilot, Entra Suite, and Agent 365.
The more material concern discussed was the shift toward token-based AI consumption through products such as Cowork and Scout. These were positioned as the real “floodgate” risk because usage-based AI models introduce variable and potentially difficult-to-forecast costs. The client was particularly concerned about how quickly this world could emerge, whether adoption is inevitable, and how to control potential usage blowouts once token-based services are enabled.
	Conclusion reached: E7 should be evaluated as part of the broader Microsoft strategy, but the client’s most important forward-looking risk is not E7 licensing itself — it is token governance, token transparency, and usage control.
2. Cowork and Scout introduce a new cost model that is hard to forecast
A major part of the discussion focused on Cowork and Scout, which were described as token-based offerings. The client noted that Microsoft had not yet raised Cowork or Scout prominently in its negotiations, leading to a discussion about why Microsoft may not be leading with these products yet. The view shared was that Microsoft may first want customers to increase adoption of Copilot and AI usage generally, then introduce more advanced token-based capabilities once AI usage becomes more embedded in day-to-day workflows.
The discussion covered how token costs can be affected by several variables:
	• The number of users enabled.
	• The number and type of AI tasks performed (lightweight, medium-weight, or heavyweight).
	• Whether users need to re-run prompts because the AI output was incomplete or incorrect.
	• Whether Microsoft changes the underlying rate card or consumption assumptions.
	• Whether usage is monthly or annual and whether unused credits expire.
A specific concern was raised that even if a customer negotiates a discount on tokens, that discount can be undermined if the vendor later changes how many tokens a given action consumes. This was compared with ServiceNow’s Now Assist model, where the screen-shared materials showed different AI actions and agentic workflows consuming different quantities of assists/actions.
	Conclusion reached: The client should treat token economics as a distinct commercial and governance workstream, not simply as an extension of the E7 renewal.
3. Token transparency is essential before the client can forecast or govern usage
The client asked whether Microsoft provides sufficiently detailed information on how many credits or tokens different queries consume, including different types of prompts and model choices. The discussion highlighted that token transparency is critical for forecasting and governance. Without a clear rate card, the client cannot reliably model consumption or explain the financial implications to decision-makers.
A Gartner slide was shown that explained Copilot Chat credit consumption examples, including different categories such as web-grounded answers, generative answers, graph-grounded prompts, and agent actions. The client also raised concerns about whether Microsoft’s current tooling provides enough visibility over spending before a query is run, rather than only explaining cost after the fact.

	• What actions consume credits and how much each type of action consumes.

1) Early renewal vs. standard renewal – core decision tension
	• The client is facing a forced trade-off: 
		○ Early renewal (by June 30) to lock in the current model (no AI bundle)
		○ Wait until September renewal, which introduces new SKU structures with embedded AI
	• The early renewal is being positioned by ServiceNow as time-sensitive due to SKU changes after June 30, specifically for ITOM.
	• However, there are inconsistencies in the vendor narrative: 
		○ Some SKUs (e.g. ITSM Standard) appear unchanged in both scenarios, which contradicts the claim that all licensing is shifting.
		○ This raises concerns that the urgency may be partially commercial pressure rather than strictly technical necessity.
👉 Why it matters:
This is a classic vendor pressure tactic—forcing a decision before the client has full clarity. The risk is committing to a structure without understanding long-term implications.
2) Shift to AI-bundled licensing – structural impact
	• ServiceNow is moving toward bundled licensing models (e.g. “Advanced” and “Prime”) that include AI capabilities by default.
	• Two major issues highlighted: 
		○ Customers who don’t need AI are forced to buy it
		○ Customers who do need AI may find included capacity insufficient, with overage costs applying
	• AI usage is allocated in units (e.g. “assists”), with additional charges for over-consumption
👉 Why it matters:
This fundamentally changes how value is consumed:
	• Less flexibility (no more selective add-ons)
	• Potential for overprovisioning or unexpected consumption costs
	• Requires much stronger demand forecasting and usage validation
3) Pricing dynamics and market benchmarks
	• The client received a ~16% increase, which is: 
		○ Within expected range based on observed market trends (typical CPI-style uplift ~15%)
		○ Lower than some more aggressive renewal proposals seen in the market (30%+)
	• However: 
		○ Moving to the new bundled model could result in materially higher effective increases (~30% range) based on comparable deals (especially in ITSM transitions)
👉 Why it matters:
The current proposal may look reasonable in isolation, but:
	• It may mask a larger structural increase under the new model
	• Benchmarking and SKU normalisation will be critical before committing
4) Reseller model shift – significant commercial change
	• The client shared that ServiceNow is now requiring renewals to go through a reseller/partner model rather than direct
	• This was unexpected and not previously aligned to Gartner guidance
	• Raises concerns: 
		○ Potential pricing opacity or markups
		○ Confusion around value (client is still paying ServiceNow for support while transacting via partner)
👉 Why it matters:
If validated, this is a material go-to-market shift:
	• Changes negotiation dynamics
	• Introduces another commercial layer
	• May reduce transparency and direct leverage with ServiceNow
5) Internal client constraints and readiness
	• The client is not operationally ready to execute an early renewal: 
		○ Requires legal review, executive (CEO) approval, and internal validation
		○ Key stakeholder is on leave and ownership is temporary
	• Questions remain on: 
		○ Licence volumes (e.g. whether ITOM Advanced quantities are appropriate)
		○ Inclusion of modules not actively used (e.g. vulnerability response)
👉 Why it matters:
Even if the early deal were attractive, execution risk alone makes it unlikely to succeed.
✅ Key Conclusions from the Call
	• Early renewal is high pressure and high uncertainty
	• There are multiple inconsistencies and unanswered questions in the supplier positioning
	• The client is not operationally prepared to execute by the deadline
	• Consensus leaning toward: 
		○ De-prioritising the early renewal
		○ Focusing on a more structured September negotiation

	Conclusion reached: The client should treat token economics as a distinct commercial and governance workstream, not simply as an extension of the E7 renewal.

Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: 🧠 Detailed key discussion points and decisions
1) The client’s main objective was to validate whether the current proposals are commercially and strategically sound
Source: meeting transcript
The client explained that they are currently under a three-year ServiceNow agreement that expires at the end of this year, and they are evaluating an expansion of capabilities, particularly ITOM and MCO, with a likely need to move on some of this work mid-year. They shared that they have been in ongoing discussions with ServiceNow, but each round of engagement appears to have increased the quoted price. They are therefore looking for benchmarking, broader market context, and guidance on how to think about a direct ServiceNow route versus a partner-led CSP proposal from LTM.
Why this matters:
This framed the entire call: the client was not simply asking whether one quote looked “good” or “bad”; they were asking how to interpret the offer in the context of typical renewals, product changes, expected vendor behaviour, and the trade-off between price and partner value.
Conclusion reached:
The discussion landed on the view that the quoted structure was not entirely out of line with the market, but there were specific areas where the client likely still had room to improve the outcome, particularly around ITOM / ITOM AI Ops.
2) The conversation distinguished between two different types of commercial increase: unit price movement and total deal movement
Source: meeting transcript
A key theme in the discussion was that ServiceNow negotiations need to be assessed in two separate ways:
	• Unit price increases on individual products/SKUs
	• Total deal uplift across the overall agreement
The point made in the meeting was that ServiceNow can be “creative” in how it drives value increases, meaning a quote may appear acceptable in one area while still producing a much larger overall uplift at the deal level.
Why this matters:
This is important because it prevents the client from assessing the renewal too narrowly. Even if some lines appear reasonable in isolation, the full commercial impact may still be more aggressive than it first appears.
Conclusion reached:
The client should evaluate the deal holistically, not just SKU by SKU, and should continue to pressure-test where the largest uplift is coming from.
3) The ServiceNow direct proposal was viewed as broadly benchmarked, but ITOM stood out as the main challenge area
Source: meeting transcript
During the review of the ServiceNow offer, the clearest area of concern identified in the transcript was ITOM / ITOM AI Ops. The discussion suggested that this portion of the quote appeared to have more room for negotiation than the rest of the package. By contrast, some other elements were described as already coming to the table relatively well versus what is being seen elsewhere in the market.
Why this matters:
This gives the client a concrete negotiation priority. Rather than spreading effort evenly across every line item, the discussion narrowed in on the area most likely to move and most likely to improve the overall position.
Conclusion reached / working position:
The strongest commercial pushback should be concentrated on ITOM, as that appears to be the most promising source of improvement in the current proposal.
4) The LTM CSP / partner option brought additional flexibility and support value, but was not inherently commercially superior
Source: meeting transcript
The client explained that LTM had provided a CSP proposal and positioned it with additional value elements, including support, added features, flexibility around usage/true-ups, and broader implementation support. In the discussion, it was noted that partner proposals often need to justify any premium by clearly showing where the buyer receives extra value, whether through support, implementation, flexibility, bundled capabilities, or other services.

Date: 14-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19449582
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Healthcare
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architecture - Other Role
Purpose: ServiceNow (SERVICENOW INC.) Proposal Review
Question Asked: Type of Purchase: New agreement
Vendor: ServiceNow (SERVICENOW INC.)
Type of Proposal: Software

Client wants advice on: 
  - Review deal to identify strategies to optimize total spend and increase efficiencies
  - Payment analysis (terms/schedule/financing, etc.)

Background and expected outcomes: 
Client typically does a three-year contract renewal with ServiceNow. However, we also requested a one-year renewal. Attached are the specifics for both options. The client would like to review with an analyst
Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: 🧠 Detailed key discussion points (context, why it matters, conclusions)
1. Nature of the renewal: like‑for‑like, not a transformation
	• What was discussed: The client confirmed the proposal is effectively a like‑for‑like renewal of the current ServiceNow environment. There are no material functional or scope changes planned at this time.
	• Why it matters: Like‑for‑like renewals provide limited natural leverage with ServiceNow, as the vendor typically expects either expansion or uplift at renewal.
	• Conclusion: Any improvement in outcome will need to come from commercial strategy and contract structuring, not from a change in requirements or roadmap.
2. Existing positioning already above peer norms
	• What was discussed: It was highlighted that the client’s current ITSM positioning is already above what is typically seen for comparable organizations, which complicates attempts to materially realign terms without a trade.
	• Why it matters: When a customer is already positioned above peer benchmarks, ServiceNow is unlikely to “reset” terms absent a compelling reason such as scope change, competitive threat, or structural change.
	• Conclusion: Expectation-setting was important here: the discussion shifted from “resetting to market” to containing future exposure and improving structural flexibility.
3. Vendor behavior and renewal dynamics
	• What was discussed: ServiceNow’s broader commercial behavior was discussed, including their focus on total relationship value, expectation of growth, lack of transparency, and increasing pressure through packaging and portfolio changes.
	• Why it matters: This context explains why standard renewal arguments often stall and why more creative or defensive strategies are required.
	• Conclusion: The client should assume a firm posture from ServiceNow and plan accordingly, rather than expecting concessions through a standard renewal motion.
4. Primary levers available to the client
Two realistic leverage paths were explored:
a) Scope and consumption pressure
	• Discussion: Reducing licenses or pulling back usage was discussed as a way to force a re‑evaluation of the commercial position. While unit metrics may adjust, total exposure can still improve.
	• Conclusion: This is a credible lever if reductions are operationally defensible.
b) Structural licensing alternatives
	• Discussion: An alternative licensing construct (unrestricted-style user model with back‑end role control) was raised as a way to reframe the conversation and reduce ongoing administrative friction.
	• Conclusion: This is not a default recommendation, but it is worth testing as a comparative scenario to create optionality.
5. Adding new functionality purely for leverage
	• What was discussed: The idea of adding additional ServiceNow functionality to offset renewal pressure was explored.
	• Why it matters: While this can sometimes stabilize renewal outcomes, it introduces long-term risk if the capability is not genuinely required.
	• Conclusion: Adding functionality only to influence renewal terms is not advisable unless there is clear intent to adopt and use it.
6. Competitive pressure and alternatives
	• What was discussed: The client raised sustainability concerns and asked how ServiceNow typically responds to competitive pressure and what alternatives exist.
	• Why it matters: Even partial competitive threats (e.g., ITSM-only alternatives) can materially shift the negotiation dynamic.
	• Conclusion: While no single competitor fully replaces the entire ServiceNow footprint, targeted alternatives are viable leverage tools.
7. Product and packaging change risk
	• What was discussed: Changes in ServiceNow’s ITSM packaging were noted as an ongoing risk factor that can be used to force customers into new constructs over time.
	• Why it matters: Delaying or passively renewing increases exposure to imposed changes later.
	• Conclusion: Renewal timing

Analyst Name: Domenico Scriva
Discussion Summary: Meeting Summary
1) Detailed key discussion points and decisions made
Source for this section: meeting transcript
A. Current commercial model: MSP vs direct with ServiceNow
A major part of the conversation focused on whether the client should remain with the current MSP model through Infosys or consider moving directly to ServiceNow for future renewals and transformation activity.
The client explained that the existing information provided reflects the current environment, while the future state is likely to involve both growth in licensing and consolidation of ServiceNow instances as part of a broader transformation programme. That matters because the right commercial route may depend not just on price, but on the level of support, transparency and flexibility needed during that transformation.
The discussion landed on an important conclusion:
	• If the client needs greater direct involvement from ServiceNow during transformation, then a direct relationship may offer more strategic flexibility.
	• If the client values a more hands-on managed support model and is satisfied with what the partner provides operationally, the MSP route may still be appropriate.
There was no final decision to switch models during the call. However, the parties did align on the need to evaluate both models more rigorously before renewal planning advances further.
B. Lack of transparency in the current MSP arrangement
The client raised a concern that the current MSP arrangement does not provide enough visibility into unit pricing or baseline licensing. This was one of the central commercial issues discussed.
That matters because without a transparent baseline, it becomes difficult for the client to:
	• compare current costs with a direct vendor relationship,
	• understand whether they are getting competitive commercial value,
	• assess whether the MSP premium is justified by additional services and support.
A practical conclusion was reached here: the current model should be assessed not only on licensing economics, but also on what the MSP is bundling in and whether those services are actually valuable enough to justify reduced transparency.
C. Whether ServiceNow can truly “see” the client’s estate under an MSP model
The client asked whether the MSP model prevents ServiceNow from seeing the client’s baseline. This became an important point because the client had heard that ServiceNow could not quote directly or lacked visibility under the MSP structure.
During the discussion, a contradiction emerged:
	• On one hand, the client had been told that ServiceNow does not have visibility of the licensing baseline under the MSP model.
	• On the other hand, ServiceNow was reportedly producing compliance/audit-style reports indicating the client may be non-compliant.
That contradiction mattered because it undermines the credibility of the explanations the client has been receiving from both parties. If ServiceNow can generate reporting indicating non-compliance, then they appear to have at least some meaningful visibility into usage or entitlement patterns.
The practical conclusion reached in the call was that the client should challenge both Infosys and ServiceNow to explain this inconsistency clearly.
D. Audit and compliance dispute
A significant portion of the call focused on the client’s concerns around audit reporting, compliance exposure, and possible changes in licensing interpretation.
The client explained that ServiceNow had apparently identified potential non-compliance and that the overage being referenced was more than 1 million in licence overage value. The concern was not simply the magnitude, but how that position had been reached. The client stated that at the beginning of the contract, their own dashboards matched the criteria provided by ServiceNow and Infosys. Now, using what they believed to be the same logic, their internal numbers no longer match the vendor/partn

Analyst Name: Nicholas Carter
Discussion Summary: Key ask:
To obtain expert insights and recommendations on effective pricing models for AI-powered BPO services, focusing on outcome-based, consumption-based, and blended approaches.

Summary:
- Ali Izic introduced M Plus Group and Ria, highlighting their AI agent platform and interest in outcome-based pricing models.
- The main inquiry centered on trends and challenges in outcome-based pricing, especially for BPO and AI-driven customer experience solutions.
- Nicholas Carter expressed skepticism toward outcome-based pricing for software products, favoring it only for defined projects.
- He explained that outcome-based pricing can create difficulties in repricing after outcomes are achieved, limiting revenue growth.
- Nicholas provided a case where improved efficiency led to reduced vendor revenue, illustrating the downside of contingency pricing.
- He noted that outcome-based pricing can lengthen sales cycles and requires robust instrumentation to measure and prove outcomes.
- Nicholas advocated for ROI-focused discussions instead, emphasizing the need to demonstrate value without tying pricing directly to outcomes.
- He highlighted a market shift toward consumption-based pricing, with AI tokens becoming a metered utility similar to telecom models.
- Nicholas observed that both buyers and sellers are accustomed to per-user, per-month models, making the transition to consumption models challenging.
- He stressed that vendors must help customers manage and predict costs, requiring strong delivery teams and transparent usage tracking.
- Nicholas described emerging trends where vendors aim for deterministic production environments to control token consumption and offer fixed pricing.
- He referenced platform companies like ServiceNow and Salesforce adopting credit-based, drawdown pricing models, though transparency remains an issue.
- In BPO, Nicholas acknowledged blended models combining people and technology, with milestone-based pricing and gain-share structures still common.
- The conversation concluded with plans for follow-up discussions and sharing of relevant Gartner research and slides.

Date: 14-May-26
Reference Number: 20029473
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: Divisional Technology Leader
Purpose: WR: AI Agent 成本计算
Question Asked: How is the development cost of a single AI Agent typically calculated in the industry? (For no-code development platforms like Coze, Dify, and n8n) Is there a universally accepted calculation method? For example: Agent application development cost = average labor cost for agent development + average computing power cost (token cost) consumed during development and testing phases.
Analyst Name: Kelli Smith
Discussion Summary: Written response sent. 

Xi,
Thank you for your request for a written response relating to the development cost of a single AI agent, specifically for No-Code Agent Builder platforms. 
The development cost of an AI agent comprises more than just the average labor cost plus token consumption during development and testing phases. Typically, we see a blended cost model encompassing:
•	Labor costs: This includes deployment, training technical, and business users, managing the full lifecycle of an agent, and continuous evaluation to maintain agent quality and reliability.
•	Compute costs: Primarily token consumption related to inference during agent runtime, but also including data ingestion, integration, and storage costs.
•	Licensing and platform fees: No-code AI agent builders do not have consistent pricing. Pricing ranges from platform fees to credits or consumption-based models, impacting total cost depending on usage patterns. Some vendors are also starting to shift to value- or outcome-based pricing.
•	Operational and governance costs: In some cases, there may be additional fees for security, compliance, monitoring, API calls, tool integration, and incident management.
A recommended costing framework emphasizes calculating cost per completed task or business outcome (e.g., cost per ticket resolved or document processed, etc.), rather than raw token cost alone. This business-aligned approach links expenditure directly to agent impact. As a best practice, Gartner encourages customers to define a blended cost per use case instead of relying on a simple additive formula (e.g., labor cost plus token cost), incorporating operational and indirect costs for accuracy. Please see: How to Build AI Agents That Deliver Sustained Business Value, With AI Agents, You Need a New Way to Calculate Cost and Value, and How CIOs Can Demonstrate AI’s Business Value Using Existing Business Metrics. 
Note that unlike traditional software, there isn’t a widely accepted formula for calculating the cost of a single AI agent or even the ‘development’ of an agent. Costs can vary significantly depending on:
•	The complexity of workflows (simple automations vs. multi-agent orchestration)
•	The degree of customization of pre-built agents or the complexity involved in creating new agents (while no-code platforms abstract much of the complexity, time is still required for testing, integrations, etc.)
•	Depth of integration (APIs, data sources, enterprise systems, etc.)
Most importantly, it is important to have robust cost governance, including token consumption controls, budgeting, FinOps integration, and security oversight, to manage total cost effectively and avoid overruns.
Many established vendors in the No-Code Agent Builder space (e.g., Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow, etc.) provide FinOps capabilities within their platforms. Some smaller vendors, such as Relevance AI and Writer, also offer FinOps capabilities, while others (e.g., Dify) may not yet have fully-robust product capabilities in this area.
I would also be happy to share more detail in an inquiry. One of the research insights that I am writing is how top product organizations benchmark AI agent impact, some of the case studies involve product teams of NCAB technology vendors that are building agents for use internally. This research is written for product leaders and leverages Gartner case-based research.

Discussion Summary: 1) Detailed key discussion points
A. The call focused on helping the client understand the structure of the proposal — not just the numbers
Source: meeting transcript
A major theme throughout the discussion was that the client was not only trying to validate whether the proposal looked commercially reasonable, but also trying to understand how the proposal was constructed. The conversation repeatedly came back to three underlying questions:
	1. How ServiceNow is structuring key components of the proposal
	2. Whether certain items are truly necessary
	3. How the client can assess whether the commercial model aligns with expected usage
This matters because the client is not simply trying to compare line items in isolation — they are trying to avoid committing to a pricing and product structure that may not reflect how they will actually deploy or consume the offering.
A clear constraint raised during the call was that the client had only provided limited underlying data, and in some cases the bill of materials was hidden, partially redacted, or expressed in percentages rather than directly comparable units. That meant the guidance provided in the meeting was intentionally framed as broad benchmark-based guidance, rather than precise validation of the client’s exact construct.
Conclusion reached:
The discussion established that the client can use the benchmark guidance directionally, but more complete internal data would be needed to tighten the analysis and confirm whether some of the proposed structures are appropriate.
B. Raptor DB emerged as a central area of concern
Source: meeting transcript + meeting chat
Raptor DB was one of the biggest discussion points in the session. The client raised several concerns around it, including:
	• whether it is actually required for the client’s Agentic AI ambitions,
	• how it is being priced or measured,
	• and how the client can ensure that the associated fees are aligned with actual usage.
These concerns were reinforced in the meeting chat, where the client explicitly posted:
	• “Do we really require Raptor DB for Agentic AI?”
	• “What are the different pricing schemes?”
	• “How can we ensure that the fees are in line with the usage (for Raptor DB)?”
The conversation made clear that this is not just a commercial question. It is also partly a technical and architectural question. The client indicated that they had previously understood Raptor DB more as an architecture-related item rather than a major negotiation sticking point, but in this proposal it had become much more material and therefore deserved closer scrutiny.
There was also some confusion during the call around how the item should be interpreted structurally — whether it should be considered more like a percentage-based platform charge or something that can be rationalised into a usage-based construct. That ambiguity itself became one of the key takeaways from the discussion.
Conclusion reached:
No final answer was reached on Raptor DB during the call. Instead, the conclusion was that this item needs further follow-up, both to validate necessity and to better understand the underlying logic of the construct.
C. Support tiers were discussed as a strategic decision, not just an add-on
Source: meeting transcript
Another important discussion area was the support model, particularly the difference between Impact Guided and Impact Total.
The client explained that one of the arguments being used internally or by the vendor was that, because of the broader Agentic AI direction, they may need a higher-touch support model and therefore the highest tier was being positioned as appropriate.
The conversation pushed back on the assumption that the highest tier should be adopted immediately. The discussion highlighted that many organisations are not typically operating on the highest level of support from the outset, and that the client should avoid overcommittin

Date: 17-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20102533
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: Cost Optimisation Scenarios
Question Asked: As a follow up to SR 19476283 w/ Stephen O'Malley, Jen has shared 3 scenarios that her and her team are working through. Jen is seeking guidance from Stephen on how to approach the 3 scenarios from a Cost Optimisation perspective and highly appreciates Stephen's public sector experience. 

1.Protecting the run under sustained cost pressure – how to prioritise essential operations versus discretionary enhancement when the branch has inherited unfunded responsibilities across critical enterprise platforms, while managing increasing BAU demand and constrained budgets.
2.ServiceNow growth outpacing its funding model – how to respond when platform adoption, contract renewal risk and unrecovered sustainment costs converge into a structural budget problem.
3.Legacy dual-running as a source of cost leakage – how to manage rising legacy sustainment and decommissioning costs when the replacement program is delayed and exit costs were underestimated upfront.
Analyst Name: Stephen O'Malley
Discussion Summary: Our conversation today focused on budget management techniques.

Key Takeaways: 

•	I recommended considering management of costs from both a supply and demand perspective. 

•	From the demand perspective, I suggested the need for robust demand management practices to align both spend and activity to the value required by the organisation. The intent of this is to make sure that you are only doing the work that everyone agrees is adding value, and low priority or misaligned work can be deprioritised or eliminated. Usually the first filter is whether the work aligns to strategy and strategic outcomes required.

You made the great suggestion of ensuring there is a clear work acceptance process into your Branch, which will help you in managing capacity and ensuring alignment.

I followed this by recommending that when you are asked to deliver something that is ‘additional’ you track and document those requests – both from the perspective of future work planning, but also to ensure you have reasons for any budget over-runs.

Certainly I would be asking the questions of those assigning you new work of how it should be prioritised, and what should be de-prioritised to allow that work to proceed, or alternatively whether new funding will be provided – but I know this is often difficult.

•	From the supply side, I suggested planning your capacity in a different way. If you know that you will be challenged by 10% of new ad hoc requests, then plan for 90% capacity in performing day to day work, in order to accommodate these requests. This gives you capacity and capability to apply to those new tasks.

Secondly I recommended considering whether each team is managing their platform effectively – do they have their systems optimised so that the minimum time and effort needs to be spent administering systems and conducting maintenance. The more you keep it simple, the easier it is to manage. Try to eliminate complexity that drives higher maintenance effort.

•	Finally we spoke about trying to change the narrative. Focus on reporting business value. Make it clear what business outcomes you deliver or facilitate. Start to make it clear what a budget cut means for the organisation (ie what does it mean for what you deliver for everyone else, not what you do). Try to make yourself a value or profit centre – not a cost centre. If the value delivered is clear and understood, it makes it harder to just cut the budget. Instead of a simple budget cut, you are making the decision to take away something that people value.

My Recommendations (in priority order) based on our discussion are: 

The following material will assist:

•	Toolkit: Portfolio Demand Prioritization and Resource Planning – speaks to demand management and resource planning. It does so in the context of PMO, but the techniques are translatable.

•	The Fundamentals of Demonstrating the Business Value of IT – focuses on business value

•	Map IT Value Stories to Business Outcomes That Matter – mapping activity to business value.

If you are interested in an additional session with a Gartner Expert, please click here or contact your account team. 

I hope the discussion was valuable, and if I can be of further assistance, please don’t hesitate to request a further discussion.

Marc Godsey is interested in implementing Software Asset Management (SAM) with ServiceNow to optimize license savings and manage true-ups effectively. Analyst Name: Matt Baldino
Discussion Summary: Background, Objectives, and Timelines
	• Challenges & Goals: The SOW lists qualitative goals, such as decommissioning legacy systems, optimizing SaaS subscription spend, and reducing audit costs. However, it fails to define quantifiable, measurable goals (e.g., specific percentage reductions in costs), which the checklist recommends to clearly convey what will make the project successful.
	• Phases, Milestones & Duration: The project has an estimated duration of 20 weeks and notes that a kickoff will occur 15 business days after signing. However, the milestones are entirely time-based (Months 1 through 5) rather than logically split by project phases (like Design, Test, and Deploy).
	• Ability to Pause: The SOW does not include a "pause clause" allowing NRG Energy to temporarily suspend the project without financial liability, which is a recommended best practice.

Scope and Deliverables
	• Scope Definition: The SOW does a good job of explicitly listing what is "In Scope" (e.g., SaaS License Management, integrations with Microsoft and Adobe) and what is "Out of Scope" (e.g., custom SaaS integrations, mobile app for SAM).
	• Deliverables Table: The SOW lacks a separate, explicit table detailing all functional and technical deliverables with their corresponding acceptance criteria, milestones, owners, and approvers, which the checklist strongly advises.
	• System Environment: The SOW lists prerequisites like having ServiceNow Xanadu and a configured CMDB, but lacks detailed system diagrams or volumetrics.

Acceptance Framework
	• Confirmed vs. Default Acceptance (Critical Risk): The SOW states that if NRG Energy does not return the Project Acceptance Form within 15 days, they "shall be deemed to have accepted all Deliverables".  Warned against this default acceptance language and recommends mandating explicit confirmation for all deliverables.
	• Defect Resolution: The SOW mentions that the customer is responsible for unit and acceptance testing, but fails to define a clear process for logging, tracking, and resolving post-delivery defects.

Resource Planning and Responsibilities
	• Named Resources & Skills: The SOW identifies the roles required (Solutions Architect, Project Manager, Business Process Consultant, Technical Consultant, Training Consultant) and notes they are "part-time". However, it does not name the specific individuals, provide their resumes, or detail their skill levels, which makes it difficult to lock in a top-tier "A team".
	• Replacement Process: There is no process outlined for replacing nonperforming provider staff.
	• RACI Table: While the SOW lists Customer Responsibilities and Duties of SHI, it does not contain a formal RACI matrix to definitively prevent overlapping accountabilities.

Project Financials
	• Payment Terms (Critical Risk): The project is a fixed fee of $171,875.00. However, the SOW requires an upfront payment of $28,645.83 upon SOW signing, and subsequent payments are tied to the completion of "Months" rather than the acceptance of specific deliverables. Strongly recommend avoiding all upfront payments and tying payments strictly to deliverable acceptance.
	• Rate Card for Future Changes: The SOW states that additional out-of-scope work will be billed at a "rate mutually agreed upon". Recommend including a pre-agreed rate card in the SOW to avoid inflated pricing for future change requests.
	• Expenses: The SOW successfully clarifies that no travel is required for the project, avoiding ambiguous travel expense clauses.

Governance and Closure
	• Governance & Escalation: While the SOW requires NRG Energy to provide a Project Manager, Platform Owner, and Subject Matter Experts, it does not document an escalation process for dispute resolution or outline a formal executive steering committee.
	• Closure & Handover: The SOW includes formal training deliverables (In-Platform Help and Quick Reference Guides). However,

Discussion Summary: Purpose:
To equip DCSA senior leadership with a clear, actionable comparison of three leading CRM/enterprise platforms—Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics, and ServiceNow—supporting rapid, strategic alignment and informed executive direction.

1. Buying Process Overview


Salesforce:

Typically involves direct engagement with Salesforce sales teams and certified partners.
Offers flexible licensing and modular purchasing options.
Emphasizes cloud-first deployment and rapid scaling.



Microsoft Dynamics:

Often procured through Microsoft enterprise agreements or partner channels.
Strong integration with existing Microsoft stack (Azure, Office 365).
Licensing can be bundled with other Microsoft products.



ServiceNow:

Direct sales model with focus on enterprise IT and workflow automation.
Implementation often involves certified ServiceNow partners.
Licensing based on modules and user types.




2. Key Factors to Consider


Business Alignment:

How well does the platform fit DCSA’s mission, workflows, and security requirements?
Does it support both current and future organizational needs?



Integration & Ecosystem:

Compatibility with existing systems (e.g., Microsoft, Oracle, legacy platforms).
Availability of APIs, connectors, and partner solutions.



Scalability & Flexibility:

Ability to adapt to evolving requirements and scale across departments.
Customization options for unique DCSA processes.



Security & Compliance:

Support for federal security standards (FedRAMP, DoD IL, etc.).
Data residency, access controls, and audit capabilities.



User Experience & Adoption:

Ease of use for end users and administrators.
Training, support, and change management resources.



Total Cost of Ownership:

Initial and ongoing costs (licensing, implementation, maintenance).
ROI and potential for cost savings through automation.




3. Key Decision Points


Strategic Fit:

Which platform best aligns with DCSA’s strategic objectives and digital transformation roadmap?



Vendor Commitment:

Strength of vendor partnership, support, and roadmap for federal clients.



Implementation Risk:

Complexity, timeline, and potential disruption during migration.



Long-Term Value:

Potential for innovation, automation, and improved mission outcomes.




4. Resources to Leverage


Gartner Research:

Magic Quadrants, Peer Insights, and Market Guides for CRM and workflow platforms.
Total cost of ownership calculators and vendor scorecards.



Federal Case Studies:

Examples of federal agencies deploying each platform.
Lessons learned and best practices.



Vendor Demos & Proof of Concept:

Request tailored demos addressing DCSA-specific requirements.
Pilot programs to validate fit and functionality.

Analyst Name: Matt Allen
Discussion Summary: Written response sent. To summarise - Organisations should avoid attempting to justify AI investments solely through FTE reduction assumptions. The most sustainable business cases combine:
Productivity improvements
Service quality enhancements
Employee experience benefits
Cost avoidance
Risk reduction

- what have you realized so far, with the current architecture? Demonstrable
- what are the required investments to change? People, processes, data, frameworks, time, contracts?
- how will the new architecture demonstrate success? Demonstrable

Date: 15-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20041413
Buyer Region: JAPAN
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: IT - Other Role
Purpose: Notes 廃止に向けた進め方・ストーリー策定についての助言依頼
Question Asked: Subject: 
Request for Guidance on Planning and Strategy for Notes Decommissioning

Question: 
In our organization, Notes has been deeply integrated into core business processes and information assets for many years. I would like advice on the following points from the perspectives of decision-making criteria and implementation approach:

What kind of “compelling rationale (story)” should we develop to engage the entire company and business units, and drive the decision and execution to decommission Notes?
Rather than simply replacing existing operations, how should we redefine processes, information, and value?

Background
The decommissioning target is the entire Dai-ichi Life Group, where each company currently uses its own implementation.
With the recent CIO transition, reducing fixed IT investment costs and reallocating resources to development and growth areas have become management priorities.
Notes is not just an email or bulletin board system; it is deeply embedded in core operations, including workflows, business processes, and inter-company replication.
Many Notes assets, developed as end-user computing (EUC), remain central to operations but lack original creators and are no longer maintainable.
Some functions have already migrated to M365 and other platforms, but there is no clear policy regarding the handling, migration, or disposal of accumulated information assets (including unstructured data) on Notes.
The absence of a clear story explaining “why change now” and “what new value will be created after migration” is the main reason for the lack of progress in decommissioning Notes.
We recognize that continuing to rely on Notes is unsustainable, especially from the perspective of future AI utilization and information management.
Although the need to move away from Notes has been discussed for about six years, the issues above have prevented concrete progress.
Analyst Name: Adam Preset
Discussion Summary: Our guidance helps Dai-ichi Life build a clear business case and phased plan to retire Lotus Notes/Domino. We focused on three areas:


Why Act Now
• Platform risk – Notes/Domino’s market share has fallen below 2 percent, making it a niche solution with less vendor investment and fewer skilled administrators.
• Hidden costs – Beyond license fees, legacy maintenance, custom-code fixes, and security or compliance gaps drive up total cost of ownership.
• Strategic upside – Decommissioning can free up an estimated 10–15 percent of application-support budget for digital insurance products, advanced analytics or AI-driven underwriting. Modern suites like Microsoft 365 unlock low-code automation, real-time analytics and Copilot-style assistants.


Rethinking Processes and Data
• Automated discovery – Use a migration scanner to inventory all Notes apps by usage, complexity and data volume.
• Business impact scoring – Rate each app on transaction volume, user base, compliance risk and strategic alignment. Prioritize scores of 4–5 for rebuild or migration.
• Selective modernization – Avoid mass rehosting. Redesign high-impact workflows with modern tools (Power Automate, Power BI, Copilot) to maximize efficiency.
• Data cleanup – Work with compliance to classify data. Archive uncertain or low-value items to a controlled repository, monitor access, and delete after 12 months of inactivity.


Mobilizing Stakeholders
• RACI structure – Define who is Responsible (IT migration team), Accountable (CIO and business leads), Consulted (security, compliance, finance) and Informed (end users, HR).
• Executive sponsors – Engage CIO, CFO, heads of operations and digital innovation with concise dashboards showing “risk if we stay” versus “value if we move.”
• Phased roadmap – Pilot one high-impact app (3–6 months), migrate top 20 percent by impact (6–18 months), then scale out and decommission the rest (18+ months).


#value Dai-ichi’s team now has a clear, step-by-step rationale and framework for prioritizing, designing and executing the Notes decommissioning with measurable business outcomes.

•	May 28 Heineken_Ticket Deflection Strategy

•	May 28 Heineken BAFO Notes

Analyst Name: Matt Baldino
Discussion Summary: Reviewed the updated BAFO offer from Unisys.  There were some really stand-out hidden risks in this engagement.  Though it was clear Unisys had brought most if not all aspects of pricing down, there were 4 areas where channels that should be low cost (Self-service, web portal resolved, etc.) were higher costs than phone/chat support.  This was across all LATAM and Spanish/Portugal support. Coupled with this, a high assumption of ticket deflection/reduction relied on this better channel utilization.  As is, this could stand in the face of the entire agreement - if the client shifts lots to self service in this geos, then they will end up paying MORE per month each year, not less.
Flat pricing for ticket volume was provided and hides this potential increase, assuming that the 44% ticket deflection would unanimously decrease pricing.

Less impactful but still important was the tooling assumptions.  Unisys had hinged the deflection perform on the org licensing the genAI and AI products from ServiceNow, something that needs to be accounted for in the TCO of this initiative. 

Penalties were too low to be impactful to the provider, they also had 90% earn back potential, and a gain share mechanism that provided them the larger pool to benefit from a flat percentage gain share )11% extra due if target reached to provide, 11% of gap in achievement back to client if target is under performed. 11% of a bigger pie to the provider, only 11% of the gap back to the client.

Date: 23-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20150502
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Transportation
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architecture - Other Role
Purpose: ServiceNow AI Integration
Question Asked: Stuart is interested in understanding the current trends and best practices in ServiceNow's AI integration, particularly in how it positions itself in the AI market. He is seeking insights into whether ServiceNow's AI capabilities live up to the marketing hype and how they compare to competitors. Questions are - What are the upcoming trends and current best practices in ServiceNow's AI integration? Is ServiceNow's AI platform delivering on its promises, or is it just a marketing strategy? How does ServiceNow's AI integration compare to other AI solutions in the market?

Update 6/18:
Confirmed the client is looking to discuss ServiceNow for ITSM.
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Stuart,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding AI in ServiceNow. I’ve done my best to answer your questions below, but please feel free to reach out if you need anything else.

The main components in ServiceNow's AI toolkit worth knowing by name are Now Assist for generative capabilities, and Predictive Intelligence.  Now Assist will help with tasks like generating or summarizing content, and natural language search.  Predictive Intelligence is the older ML capability that handles tasks that can be predicted using historical data, like ticket classification and routing.
Now Assist for ITSM specifically targets incident triage, generating summaries, and resolution recommendations.  So when your human agents pick up a ticket, they get a summarized incident history and the suggested resolution steps based on similar past incidents.  Deflection rates on resolution suggestions vary widely depending on how well the flows are built and documented.  The more successful orgs invest time tuning automated resolution workflows instead of focusing on AI output.
ServiceNow's latest approach is agentic AI.  It's identical to how agentic systems work in other platforms, and whether built in ServiceNow or in something like Copilot, agents can communicate through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.  The idea is that external AI agents can now execute governed actions inside ServiceNow without going through the UI.  This is helpful if you have business units that depend on data or workflows in ServiceNow, but they don't typically access the platform directly.
Does the marketing match reality?  Somewhat.  Features like summarization and routing work reasonably well if you have enough historical data, but none of the AI features work well if you don't have good data or a well-defined workflow.  Much of the upfront investment in AI is simply cleaning data before asking AI to deliver.  ServiceNow's demos work fine because they are showing overly simplistic use-cases with bespoke input data.  However, reality for production environments is a lot messier.
The adoption numbers are very real, but we still don't have data on the value being generated from these AI investments in ServiceNow.  Also, some of their growth could reflect repackaging of existing capabilities under the Now Assist brand rather than net-new AI value.  Based on discussions with my clients, very few have achieved meaningful success with their AI implementations, but that doesn't mean there's a problem with ServiceNow's platform.  Basically, if you have the right use-cases with the right data, you can still achieve a positive ROI even with the insane pricing, but it is tough.
You should confirm with your sales rep exactly which AI features are included in your proposed package, because they are not all available on every tier.  The generative AI features require specific SKUs and release versions, and the gap between the demo and what your contract actually includes can be significant.
ServiceNow certainly holds the advantage in terms of pure ITSM depth.  It is considered enterprise-grade ITSM, whereas something like Jira Service Management is more focused on DevOps-native environments, and Salesforce's ITSM depth is comparatively limited, performing better when focused on front-office workflows.
The two closest competitors in terms of like-for-like capabilities would be BMC Helix and ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus.  BMC Helix is another enterprise-grade ITSM tool, but it comes with a hefty price tag just like ServiceNow.  ManageEngine, on the other hand, has remained a low-cost option for decades, and it has a very similar feel to ServiceNow.  You can't go wrong with either platform; they're ITIL-compliant and actively developed to stay competitive.
The AI capabilities across all the major players are converging.  ServiceNow has more runway on the enterprise workflow automation side because the platform began its

Date: 29-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20139983
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Retail
Buyer Role: IT Procurement Manager
Purpose: Execute FinOps Best Practices
Question Asked: Chandra Caplinger is the IT Procurement Manager for O'Reilly Autoparts and aims to move from a refined FinOps charter to execution, establishing practical processes that improve visibility and reduce cloud spend across IT and the broader business. She also wants to prepare an internal presentation and alignment plan with leadership while shortlisting and comparing FinOps/CFM tools identified post–FinOps X. Questions: What step-by-step execution approach, roles, and governance should we use to operationalize our FinOps charter, including KPIs/OKRs and how engineering, finance, and operations collaborate? What decision criteria and integration considerations should guide selection among FinOps/CFM tools (e.g., Apptio, Flexera/ProsperOps, Zylo, Finout, Doit, Datadog, ServiceNow) for visibility, optimization, and automated rightsizing/spin up–down controls?
Analyst Name: Chuck Lawton
Discussion Summary: Current Environment & Challenges at O'ReillyEarly FinOps Maturity
- O'Reilly is in the very early stages of implementing a structured Technology Business Management (TBM) model and currently lacks centralized procurement, budgeting, or FinOps practices.  
- Cultural Lack of Cost Awareness: Engineering and application teams have historically operated with zero cost awareness, treating company funds like "free money" and lacking visibility into how their deployments impact the company's bottom line.  
- Antiquated Financial Reporting: The current financial data provided by the finance team is delivered via antiquated, old spreadsheets, making holistic spend visibility difficult.  
- Imminent Cloud Launch: The company currently has no live production workloads in the public cloud, but is scheduled to deploy its first live production workload in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) this July.  
- SaaS Duplication & Shadow IT: Decentralized teams frequently procure their own software via corporate credit cards without standard IT contract reviews, resulting in massive tool duplication (e.g., seven different chat tools) and highly underutilized software licenses.  
- Core Values vs. Execution: While cost control is an official core company value, O'Reilly has historically struggled to enforce the constraints needed to actually realize it.  

Strategic Guidance from Chuck
- FinOps as an Engineering Skill: Cloud Financial Management (CFM) is fundamentally an engineering capability, not an administrative or financial procurement task, because engineers make the structural spend decisions.  
- Simplified Tagging Strategy: To avoid overwhelming engineering teams, O'Reilly should use a lightweight cloud tagging strategy—ideally starting with a single application ID—to tie resources back to application owners and cost codes.  
- Maturity Framework & Low-Hanging Fruit: Applying Gartner's framework (Plan, Track, Optimize, Empower), O'Reilly should focus initial optimization on normal run-rate deviations and track Service Level Objective (SLO) adherence as a core KPI.  
- Unit Economics Maturity: As a future milestone (Year 2), Chandra should look to establish "unit economics" (e.g., cloud cost per completed customer checkout) to meaningfully elevate cost conversations with finance.  
- SaaS Management Platforms (SMP): Utilizing an SMP can help bridge the visibility gap by connecting directly to Single Sign-On (SSO) portals and identifying deltas between purchased licenses and active users.

Date: 24-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20134178
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Enterprise Architecture - Other Role
Purpose: ServiceNow Exit Strategy
Question Asked: What are the market alternatives to ServiceNow's ITSM and HR modules that can effectively replace them? How can we develop a roadmap for exiting ServiceNow while ensuring minimal disruption to our operations? Are there existing tools within our organization that can be leveraged to replace ServiceNow modules?
Analyst Name: Tyler Cheney
Discussion Summary: Hello Raina,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding ServiceNow exit strategy. I’ve done my best to answer your questions below, but please reach out if you need further assistance.
On the ITSM side, the most popular alternatives are Jira SM, Freshservice, BMC Helix, ManageEngine, and HaloITSM.  Jira SM is the most popular for teams that heavily rely on Atlassian tools, and it handles incident, problem, and change management reasonably well.  It won't match ServiceNow's depth or breadth, but for most small-to-medium orgs, that depth is overkill anyway.  Freshservice is worth a look if you want something more turnkey with less configuration.  It's lighter, faster to deploy, and the UI is more forgiving for users.  BMC Helix is the other enterprise-grade option if you need something that competes with ServiceNow feature-for-feature, though you're trading one complex platform for another, which may or may not be the point.  ManageEngine is a reasonable option if cost is a driving factor.  The ITSM module is competent across the core ITIL processes and it integrates well with the rest of their suite, though the UI and overall polish lag behind the newer platforms.  HaloITSM is a really solid product out of the box.  It's default configuration is great, which I believe is why it's been gaining popularity with mid-size orgs.
The HR module is different because ServiceNow HRSD isn't typically the system of record.  It's usually sitting on top of something like Workday or SAP, handling case management and employee-facing services.  If that's what you have now, replacing HRSD is more about picking a case management or self-service tool than replacing an HR platform.  Workday has its own case and knowledge management capabilities now and has matured considerably.  If you're already licensed for Workday, it's worth pressure-testing whether those native features cover your requirements before shopping for something else.  SAP SuccessFactors is similar.
For exiting ServiceNow, the roadmap usually begins by taking an audit of what you're actually using today.  ServiceNow tends to accumulate a lot of configuration and customization over time, and no one ever has a clear picture of which modules or custom content are actively in use versus which ones people work around.  From there, the general approach is phased by module and by risk.  Incident and request ticketing are usually the first to migrate because the workflows are relatively standardized and you need the ability to log incidents and requests from day 1.  Change and problem tickets carry a little more risk because they typically have more complex requirements, so you want to migrate those after the platform has built some capability and trust is improved.  HR workflows tend to affect a broader user base and need foundational stability, so those typically go last when change management is present to support them.
Data migration can be easy or difficult depending on what data you want to keep.  Historical ticket data is usually a simple migration because it's table-to-table.  Knowledge articles can be tricky if the formatting between the two platforms is incompatible.  The CMDB is the most challenging because you are not likely to find a platform with a data model similar to ServiceNow's, and CMDBs typically contain a massive number of records.  I would plan for a data cleanse as part of the migration, and be realistic about what historical data you actually need to carry over versus what can be archived.
As for existing tools in your environment, there might be some around that aren't obvious at first.  If your organization runs Microsoft 365, you already have access to capabilities that cover some of this ground.  Azure DevOps handles ticketing and workflow reasonably well for app teams, and Power Automate can build automated workflows that integrate with many other platforms.  MS Teams is already where a lot of incident respons

- The Gartner Expert described scenarios where Agentic AI is effectively used, such as content interpretation, triage, and exception handling, which enhance productivity in processes like claims processing.
- The Expert advised evaluating the cost-benefit ratio of Agentic AI against traditional automation, suggesting transparency from vendors like UiPath regarding pricing and token consumption.
- The discussion touched on the role of vector databases in Agentic AI for context management and reducing hallucination, stressing the need for platform engineering to ensure compliance and efficiency.
- UiPath was noted as a strong player in the automation space, offering both RPA and API automation, and having expanded its capabilities through acquisitions like Cloud Elements.
- The Expert mentioned other competitors in the automation space, including ServiceNow, Microsoft, and emerging players like N8n and Tints, which offer different approaches to automation.
- The conversation concluded with a discussion on the need for a runtime platform or container to deploy and integrate agents, highlighting the infrastructure requirements for adopting Agentic AI.

CF A: The company’s defensibility as a platform over the next 3-5 years remains strong relative to others, particularly among the largest of enterprise customers (where even if someone is motivated to switch and under the best of conditions a migration can take 1-3 years or longer from ideation to execution).

I must note however meaningful competition in the core technology workflows/foundational base (ITSM/ITOM) has been growing and continues to grow (ex. Atlassian now number 3 in terms of ITSM platform share (at 10.2%, vs. SN’s 49.9%) and second in terms of YoY revenue growth (22%) in our latest Market Share data).

Q: Any data on partner ecosystem health, client retention or switching behaviour?

CF A: As noted in this recent Gartner report, there has been a notable increase in the number of Gartner clients expressing an interest in moving away from ServiceNow ITSM fueled by high licensing costs, licensing complexity and administrative costs. 

We do not have published quantitative data that I can share in this regard, however I refer back to growing growth rates of competitors (who generally are positioning lower cost and simpler solutions) and ServiceNow’s slowing/stabilizing growth rate in the ITOM markets in recent years. 

Additionally, Gartner clients have been sharing decidedly mixed experiences with the company’s AI offerings, however this is not particularly unique to vendors of similar size and complexity.

Q: Gartner’s current view on AI disruption risk to the ServiceNow ecosystem and how that compares to other enterprise platforms

CF A: On balance, ServiceNow is not particularly more or less susceptible to AI disruption risk compared to other enterprise platforms given their early and aggressive moves to incorporate the technologies into their solutions and most importantly link their use to their platform champion’s ambition/ perception of success. Generally, we see AI enhancing Enterprise Applications, not replacing them in the long term.

Less clear is how the company’s major pricing and packaging changes that effectively “force” purchase of AI capacity is received by the customer base in a time where their primary Technology Workflows competitors have much more flexible and transparent pricing.

Date: 7-May-26
Reference Number: 20000040
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Healthcare
Buyer Role: Procurement - Other Role
Purpose: Delegation of Authority
Question Asked: UPDATED 28th APRIL - A written response would be fine.

He’s trying to gauge how others, especially in healthcare, delegate purchasing authority.  For example, Directors can make a purchase up to $5K without using the formal purchasing process, VPs are $15K, etc...
----------------------------------------------------
Client is looking for information on different benchmarks for delegation of authority levels.
Analyst Name: Andrea Greenwald
Discussion Summary: First – Delegation of authority is a different decision than “not using a purchasing process”. 
-	Delegation of authority is the level of authority for approval that an individual can sign off for. 
-	Not using a purchasing process – is a buying channel and competitive bid decision. 

In both situation – you’re looking for a risk and efficiency tradeoff
 
Second – Details. 
Delegation of Authority
I’ve included the typical authority approval limits for both Purchase Order (sl 33) and Non-Purchase Order (Sl 34). Median associate directors $70k, directors $225k, VP $1M, SVP $2,25M, CFO $7.2M. Procurement Policy and Procedures Benchmark Findings Thresholds should be set based on your level of trust, risk appetite and size of budget. Also included is slide 31, which is how many approvals are needed at certain spend thresholds. [This data isn’t specific to your industry, but examples do exist at the bottom on this note]. 

Competitive Bid
For small companies typically any indirect spend with total contract value spend above $50k (or $100k-150k for large companies, and $200k for huge companies) does need to go through the full sourcing process. Rules may differ for sole source or direct awards, government regulation thresholds, rigor on the amount of spend, and size of the procurement team. Anything below this threshold would go through a different buying channel. 
 
Buying Channels – This would avoid the sourcing process and in many cases procurement wouldn’t be involved in the spend, but they would still need to “buy in the right way”  
Depending on the spend amount/category – Quick Answer: Top 8 Solutions for Managing Tail Spend 
•	PO/Non-PO
•	Catalogues/B2B
•	Tail spend solution 
•	Purchasing card 
•	AP solution/Pay methods 
•	Preferred supplier program
•	Business self-source (Ie 3 bids and a buy)
•	Outsourcing (BPO) 

Industry Examples
Boston Children’s Hospital (See page 9)
Western Health (See page 11) 

Health System A implemented expanded controls and C-suite mandates regarding financial commitments and signature authority:
•	$150,000 Threshold: All contracts (regardless of type) with a financial commitment of $150,000 or more must be reviewed by a Category Manager.
•	$250,000 Threshold: Any spend over $250,000 is mandated to engage strategic sourcing. Furthermore, the supply chain team leads the negotiations and explicitly signs off on all contracts above $250,000.

Health System B is refining its contracting processes by establishing specific dollar limits to dictate the level of review required:
•	Under $2,500 ("Low Dollar, Low Risk"): Contracts under $2,500 are handled via a quick questionnaire intake portal (ServiceNow) that allows the end-user to bypass lengthy reviews and go straight to purchasing.
•	$2,500 to $50,000: For contracts within this mid-tier range, the system is implementing an "auto pen" process. A dedicated person reviews these contracts to fast-track them, allowing contract managers to focus on higher-risk or higher-dollar agreements.

Health System C utilizes dollar limits specifically to delegate authority within its Value Analysis Teams (VAT):
•	Under $100,000: If a product or technology request does not exceed this threshold, the decision-making authority remains at the local Hospital Value Analysis Committee level.
•	$100,000 or More: If the request has a system impact of $100,000 or more, it triggers an escalation to the Corporate VAT for a system-wide decision.

Health System D has highly centralized its signatory authority within the supply chain department rather than dispersing it across the C-suite. The Assistant Vice President of Supply Chain Management serves as the main contract signatory for the organization, signing between 120 and 150 contracts per month, with very few contracts requiring a C-suite signature outside of the supply chain department.

Genesys:  Genesys would be preferable for large-scale, multi-channel deployments, strong integration partner network and deep CRM integration.
