LinkLive.ai: Limited Gartner coverage / No specific information on this vendor

Recommendation: For seamless voice-to-video migration, Glia offers a more specialized, frictionless experience; Genesys is suitable if broader multichannel orchestration is required and you want voice/digital on a single platform/vendor.

Migration from Voice to Video Interactions

Genesys provides multichannel flexibility and can support video either natively or via numerous AppExchange plugins. Video can be launched directly from web chat or entered via an SMS/Email link during a voice call (https://help.genesys.cloud/articles/video-chat/)

Alternative Vendors for Financial Services

Notable Gartner-recommended vendors include: Talkdesk (with video engagement via AWS Chime), NICE, and LivePerson (now part of Soundhound).


Recommendation: Consider these alternatives if specific capabilities (e.g., composable integrations, advanced analytics) are required beyond Genesys or Glia.

42Gears
Overview: 42Gears, headquartered in Bangalore, India, offers an endpoint management solution named SureMDM. It supports all major operating systems, including Windows client, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, Android (Enterprise, OEMConfig, and AOSP), ChromeOS, and various Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian, CentOS, SUSE Linux, Linux Mint, and Raspberry Pi OS). 42Gears specializes in rugged and shared device use cases. English is the supported language for users, technicians, and technical support.

Deployment options: Turnkey SaaS, on-premises, and managed private cloud. 

MSE context: 42Gears provides policy-driven patch management for Windows and Linux, remote troubleshooting, and hardware/software asset discovery. While lacking built-in ticketing, it integrates with ITSM platforms like ServiceNow. Additional features include management of printers and accessories, kiosk mode, app usage analytics, and remote support. SureMDM integrates with Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Samsung Knox, Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), as well as security information and event management (SIEM) tools such as Splunk and LogRhythm.

Pricing and implementation: Annual list pricing is $47.88 per device for Standard Cloud, $65.88 per device for Premium, and $95.88 per device for Enterprise. 42Gears offers add-ons for identity provider (IdP) and zero-trust access security modules. Basic support is included with all editions and implementation services are available for complex deployments at an additional cost.

Applivery
Overview: Headquartered in Madrid, Spain, Applivery supports Windows, iOS/iPadOS, macOS, and Android devices with Apple and Android eSIM management that includes remote activation and deprovisioning. It features AI-driven automation for provisioning, patching, and policy enforcement. Applivery primarily focuses on the European region but offers coverage for Latin America, the Middle East and Africa, and North America. The product supports 10 languages, with technical support available in English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Deployment options: Turnkey SaaS and on-premises hosting.

MSE context: Applivery enables full life cycle application and device management, with support for mobile application management (MAM), shared devices, and kiosk mode. Real-time reporting, prebuilt policy templates, and application delivery workflows — such as those with CI/CD tools — are included. Integrations with Okta, Auth0, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, CrowdStrike, Check Point, Bitrise, Jenkins, GitHub, and GitLab are supported.

Pricing and implementation: Annual list pricing is Starter ($27 per device), Advanced ($42 per device), and Enterprise (custom pricing). Asset management, remote control, and license management are included in the Enterprise bundle, which also includes a dedicated success manager. Implementation services include add-on professional services for premium identity integrations, phased device deployment strategies, API integrations, and workflow automation customization.


Fleet Device Management
Overview: Fleet, headquartered in San Francisco, California, is an open-source endpoint management platform that supports Windows client and server, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, Android, ChromeOS, and most Linux distributions (CentOS, Ubuntu, Fedora, Amazon, Debian, Red Hat Enterprise, openSUSE, Arch, and Omarchy). English is the supported language for users and technicians, and for technical support.

Deployment options: Fleet is delivered both as a self-hosted and SaaS solution.

Date: 1-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19444336
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Banking, Finance and Insurance
Buyer Role: IT - Other Role
Purpose: Secure User-Centric Integration & Identity
Question Asked: Background Context:
The team is moving from traditional system-to-system integrations to user-centric (agent-to-backend using user credentials) patterns. They need to understand the technical requirements for backend systems and identity providers (e.g., Okta) and want best practices for secure, scalable implementation.

Analyst Questions:

What are the technical criteria and best practices for enabling secure, user-centric integrations between agentic AI and backend systems?
How should organizations design identity and access management for agent-to-backend integrations, especially with platforms like Okta, Workday, and ServiceNow?
What are common pitfalls and solutions when implementing principal propagation or similar patterns?
Are there frameworks or checklists for upskilling teams on modern integration and identity approaches?
Analyst Name: Mehmet Yaliman
Discussion Summary: Executive Summary

Organizations transitioning to user-centric, agent-to-backend integration models must prioritize secure, standards-based identity and access management. This involves adopting modern protocols such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, implementing dynamic and context-aware authorization, and ensuring robust lifecycle management across platforms like Okta, Workday, and ServiceNow. Effective integration requires not only technical controls but also alignment between HR, IT, and security functions. Teams should focus on secure token handling, event-driven provisioning, and continuous upskilling to mitigate risks and ensure scalable, auditable operations.

1. Technical Criteria and Best Practices for Secure Agent-to-Backend Integration

Enabling secure, user-centric integrations, where agentic AI interacts with backend systems using user credentials, requires a shift from static service accounts to dynamic, delegated access patterns. The core technical criteria and best practices include:

Adoption of Standardized Modern Protocols: Organizations must utilize OAuth 2.0 for delegating access and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for adding an identity layer to verify the user. The recommended flow is the Authorization Code Grant with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE), which is especially critical for public clients such as browser-based agents, as it prevents token interception.
Strict Token Security and Lifecycles: Access tokens (typically JSON Web Tokens or JWTs) should be short-lived, expiring in seconds or minutes rather than hours, to minimize the window for exploitation if intercepted. Refresh tokens must be rigorously managed with automatic rotation upon each use.
Secure Token Storage and Handling: Agents must securely store and handle tokens, utilizing secure enclaves or OS-level credential managers where available, to further reduce the risk of credential compromise.
Proof-of-Possession: To prevent unauthorized token reuse, tokens should be sender-constrained using cryptographic mechanisms such as mutual TLS (mTLS) or Demonstration of Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), ensuring tokens are bound to the specific client that requested them.
Decoupled and Context-Aware Authorization: Separation of authentication and authorization is strongly recommended. Implementing a policy engine such as Open Policy Agent (OPA) allows systems to externalize fine-grained authorization logic, ensuring access is evaluated dynamically based on user context and zero-trust principles.

2. Designing IAM for Agent-to-Backend Integrations

To design an effective Identity and Access Management (IAM) architecture for this model, the infrastructure must support an "identity fabric" approach that synchronizes data across providers.

Okta (Identity Federation and Token Issuance): Okta should serve as the central identity provider to federate identity and issue secure OIDC and OAuth 2.0 tokens. The design must leverage Okta's advanced security features, including adaptive Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and contextual access controls, ensuring that backend token requests reflect the user's real-time security state and risk profile. Okta’s API Access Management can be used to enforce granular policies for agent-based integrations.
Workday (Lifecycle Management): Workday should act as the authoritative source for HR data, utilizing the System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM 2.0) protocol. Organizations should configure Workday to automatically trigger identity provisioning and deprovisioning events (the "joiner-mover-leaver" lifecycle) so that agent access privileges are immediately updated or revoked upon any change in employee status. To minimize the risk of orphaned accounts, ensure that HR-driven changes in Workday are immediately reflected in Okta and downstream systems via event-driven provisioning and deprovisioning, leveraging Workday’s event hooks where possible.
Servic

The reason for adding the extra questions is that for configuring an architecture, you will need a metamodel that you can align all artifacts to, with their attributes and relationships.
Servicenow has introduced CSDM 5 which expands the previous metamodel into a digital product lifecycle model. In that document, Servicenow also includes a nice graphic that maps its products/modules on the lifecycle:

 

The graphic shows the need for a variety of tools required to manage a product lifecycle. The same applies for configuring architectures, as the left shows the business architecture part, where the middle shows the technology and application portfolio focus which translates into application and technology architecture. The right side is about operations and services to deliver and operate the digital products. Note that servicenow defines services as products as well. In this lifecycle approach Serviceow positions EA at the technical and application portfolio level, focused on applications and solutions, more than operations.

When considering using Servicenow as backend it hence depends on your focus for EA – is it strategic, tactical or operational? Do you want to use Servicenow as input for strategic portfolio management, or application portfolio or technology portfolio, or a specific solution architecture? The graphic shows the kind of products or modules you would require dependent on your focus.

The simple answer is that IF you already have an EA tool, most will have either an OOTB connector with Servicenow or a potential to use a REST API to connect with Servicenow, and in most cases the tools connect to Servicenow as CMDB. 

Independent on if you have don’t have an EA tool, my suggestion is to follow the 8 Steps to Select and Obtain Value From Enterprise Architecture Tools. Especially the first steps require you to clarify what you really need, and in steps 3 and 4 you will potentially see the Servicenow connection in regard to data. Based on your metamodel – you see the extra question referring to metamodels – you might have to manually map the CMDB data to your tool metamodel and that requires agreement on the data model being used. While you refer to servicenow, having clarity on the datamodel is critical for any architecture – hence the preference for a singular metamodel to connect to and ensure within the context of your EA tool correct analysis and decisions can be made, based on reliable data.

I also added question on the impact of Servicenow pricing models on how you use and integrate with Servicenow. It’s commonly underestimated, but dependent on the modules and HOW you access them – for example with increased level of AI or agentic capabilities, pricing rapidly becomes a challenge. Hence, always consider the impact of your demand on Servicenow spend.

In terms of research, here are relevant docs to scan – note that you should also assess the links in the AskGartner doc, but these are many more than the ones below:

First, overview of Servicenow capabilities and considerations for your questions:

•	CIOs’ Guide to ServiceNow Strategy, Roadmaps and Produ

Date: 17-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19478917
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Services
Buyer Role: IT/Infrastructure and Operations - Other Role
Purpose: Observability/Monitoring - Gates Foundation
Question Asked: We are looking to understand the current market landscape of monitoring and observability capabilities.
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: These are the key takeaways I shared with the client and emailed after the call:

Preserve modular, vendor‑agnostic data ownership: Standardize telemetry (e.g., OpenTelemetry) to decouple data generation from analysis, reducing lock‑in and enabling future platform or AI changes without re‑instrumentation.
Build for collection, buy for analysis: Use open standards for telemetry collection, but rely on a commercial enterprise platform (e.g., Datadog) for scalable analytics, since building and maintaining a custom analytics backend is operationally expensive.
Consolidate overlapping observability tools: If teams are using Datadog and New Relic for similar needs, evaluate use cases and standardize on a single observability platform to improve cross‑stack visibility, simplify integrations, and control licensing costs.
Centralize AI observability early: As AI systems are introduced, avoid point‑solution monitoring and manage AI‑specific signals alongside traditional infrastructure data within the primary observability platform.
Use ThousandEyes for targeted digital experience insight: ThousandEyes can complement the observability stack with network path and endpoint visibility in hybrid Azure environments, with greater value when correlated with core platform telemetry.
Log all automated fixes in ServiceNow: Ensure every automated resolution still generates and closes a ServiceNow record to maintain an audit trail, support ROI tracking, and identify recurring or systemic issues.

ServiceNow – service portal; CMBD incl. discovery, inventory, service mapping
Analyst Name: Martin Caren
Discussion Summary: Hi Kevin,
Thank you for your time on the last call. I really enjoyed talking with you and I appreciate the good conversation and insights.
I’m sorry it’s taken a little while to get back to you – please accept my apologies. 

Here are the notes from the call, which I hope will be useful for you and the team:

Attendees:
•	Marcus Powell (Application Support Lead, DTI, City of Chicago)
•	Kevin Kirby (Head of Support, DTI, City of Chicago; seat holder)
•	Deborah Anderson (Head of Enterprise Architecture, DTI, City of Chicago)
•	Mariclaire (Gartner Account Executive)
•	Martin Caren (Observability Specialist, Gartner)

Summary:
The City of Chicago’s Department of Technology and Innovation (DTI) is transitioning to a centralized application support operating model. Historically, application support was vendor-driven, with each vendor using their own monitoring tools and processes. The goal is to standardize application support, similar to the ongoing ServiceNow ITSM onboarding, and potentially adopt a single enterprise application monitoring and observability platform for all vendors.

Technical Discussion:
•	Current tools: ServiceNow for ITSM, SolarWinds for network and server monitoring, Palo Alto for centralized firewall logging, Splunk for log monitoring, and limited use of New Relic for APM (Application Performance Monitoring).
•	Multi-cloud environment: Expansion into Azure, AWS, GCP, and Oracle Cloud, requiring observability solutions with strong multi-cloud visibility.
•	Application monitoring: Most vendors use their own tools; city-managed platforms lack mature APM capabilities.
•	Event intelligence: The team is considering event intelligence solutions (e.g., Big Panda) to centralize and correlate events from multiple sources, addressing alert fatigue and siloed data.

People and Process (Observability Perspective):
•	DTI aims to remove vendor dependency, enabling seamless transitions between vendors without changing monitoring solutions.
•	The team is open to making platform standardization a contractual requirement for vendors.
•	There is recognition of the need for an inventory of all vendor platforms and a review of contractual setups to assess feasibility of consolidation.

Key Observability Models Discussed:
1.	Multiple Vendor Tools: Flexible, but costly and fragmented.
2.	Single Platform: Simplifies management but rarely achieved due to migration costs and vendor lock-in.
3.	Primary/Secondary Platforms: Most common; critical apps monitored by a leading platform (e.g., Dynatrace, Datadog), less critical apps by secondary tools (e.g., SolarWinds).
4.	Event Intelligence Layer: Centralizes event correlation and business impact analysis, often necessary in siloed environments.
5.	Open Telemetry/Data Lake: Not currently relevant for the City of Chicago.

Market Guidance:
•	Leaders in the Magic Quadrant (Dynatrace, Datadog, New Relic, Grafana) are recommended for primary platforms.
•	SolarWinds is widely used for its price but lacks maturity compared to leaders
•	Logic Monitor and other mid-tier vendors may offer better value and roadmap than SolarWinds.
•	Proof of concept with open source or Event Intelligence tools (e.g., Big Panda) is suggested to validate requirements before full investment.

Action Points (Agreed Next Actions):
•	Martin to send key resources: Magic Quadrant, slide deck on observability models, “Key Functional Considerations” document, and a preview note on proof of value.
•	DTI to conduct an inventory of all vendor monitoring platforms and review contractual possibilities for consolidation.
•	Schedule follow-up calls: 
o	Deep dive on observability platform selection.
o	Event intelligence strategy and tools.
o	US-based Gartner expert consultation for local context and vendor insights.
•	DTI to consider proof of concept with Big Panda or similar for event intelligence.

Date: 17-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20091891
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Education
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: AI and Data Strategy Review
Question Asked: Chris’ team has developed an AI and data strategy focused on foundational enablement (“foundations, not flagships”) and seeks expert review and feedback. They are interested in a written response to their strategy document, with the option to schedule a follow-up call if the insights are actionable.

Specific Questions:
What gaps or opportunities exist in our current AI and data strategy, particularly regarding foundational enablement, risk management, and scalability in higher education?
Are there leading practices or case examples for accelerating foundational AI adoption while ensuring alignment with institutional mission and operational realities?
What future trends should we anticipate in AI governance, data integration, and vendor management that may impact our roadmap?

Intended Outcome:
Chris wants actionable feedback to refine their strategy, ensure alignment with industry trends, and identify areas for further investment or risk mitigation.
Analyst Name: Jeroen Cornelissen
Discussion Summary: Overall, the architectural primitives you have defined are excellent for scaling reliable, agentic AI. To help you refine this strategy, ensure even further alignment with broader industry trends, and mitigate potential risks, here are a few areas for you to consider:

Strengths to Double Down On: The "Three Lanes" & Ontology Ownership Your portfolio approach of the "Three Lanes" (Enterprise Platform, Design Partnerships, Homegrown) is a best-practice strategy for balancing quick wins with long-term capability building. Furthermore, your explicitly stated principle that BU retains ownership of the enterprise ontology (rather than outsourcing it to a vendor) is a critical strategic move. This ensures long-term, vendor-agnostic flexibility and correctly positions ontologies as the must-have asset for a reliable enterprise context layer.
Broadening the Scope: Moving Beyond a One-Sided IT Perspective Currently, the strategy reads very much from an IT infrastructure perspective. While IS&T has built a strong engine, you need to be sure that the rest of the car is equally developed. We recommend explicitly emphasizing that creating an "AI-Native University" requires the rest of the organization to co-steer. The overarching AI vision, AI value generation, and AI culture must be owned collaboratively across business units to successfully transition from an AI-Opportunistic to an AI-First (or AI-Native) organization. Of course, it may be possible that this is already the case, but that is out of our current purview.
Maturing AI Governance vs. AI Security Your "Built Secure by Default" framework is robust, particularly your use of identity delegation and API security. However, to truly support this transformation, the institution needs a mature AI Governance platform. This means moving beyond just IT security gates to ensure robust regulation and supervision that guards BU's broader organizational and ethical standards.
Maturing the Context Layer: Operational State & Provenance Your central framework aptly addresses Semantics through your Semantic Layer and Ontology. However, there are two operational gaps to address for a complete and reliable architecture:
Operational State (Right-Time Data): Ensure your architecture supports event-driven operational state. If agents execute multi-step tasks using batch-updated data, they risk relying on stale institutional context.
Provenance vs. Auditability: You correctly note that your Agent Layer is "auditable" (logging actions and data access). However, this should be extended to Provenance (establishing closed-loop mechanisms to track whether an agent's action resulted in a successful business outcome), and piping that feedback back into the knowledge base to continuously adapt and refine the system
Validating the "Build vs. Buy” Economics: While we agree that AI is accelerating development, we caution against the sentiment that a fundamental shift to a fully "build-first" or self-generated software model is imminent. In the short- to mid-term, organizations are highly unlikely to replace key systems of record (especially the “digital backbone” such as ERP, CRM, ServiceNow...) with self-generated software. The reality of "Build vs. Buy" in the AI era requires evaluating a few critical factors:
True Total Cost of Ownership (TCO): While the initial build cost might appear to favor building, true ownership encompasses ongoing operational maintenance, regular upgrades, and long-term lifecycle management driven by evolving underlying systems. These post-launch expenses are frequently overlooked during early planning but typically represent the most significant portion of the budget.
AI Engineering Maturity: Building and maintaining proprietary AI solutions across the board requires a level of software engineering maturity typically reserved for massive tech outliers. Because AI capabilities are rapidly commoditizing, buying off-the-shelf s
================================================================================

Date: 8-May-26
Reference Number: 19484270
Buyer Region: ASIAPAC
Buyer Industry: Energy and Utilities
Buyer Role: CIO or Head of Technology
Purpose: Review: IT Performance KPIs
Question Asked: Brent Gimpel is seeking to develop performance KPIs for IT to improve visibility and prioritization of work across teams. He aims to transition from using Excel to tools like ServiceNow or DevOps for better tracking and prioritization. Questions are - How can we effectively map IT performance measures to executive priorities such as value, risk, and cost? What benchmarks exist for areas like Digital Solutions and infrastructure to ensure our KPIs are aligned with industry standards?
Analyst Name: Srinath Sampath
Discussion Summary: Dear Brent Gimpel:





        Thank you for your inquiry on IT Performance KPIs. 



The document you shared with us for review is strong on the operational front and would be very relevant for a technology leadership audience operating review. To make it relevant to a CEO (or generally a CXO audience), it needs to be translated into an executive-friendly lens. 

Executives think in 3 general outcome lenses: value, cost and risk. You need to map your IT metrics to one (or more) of these lenses and make executive trade-offs explicit. 

Business Value of IT 
You already hint at value in multiple places in your document (data products, automation, etc.) but it needs to be made explicit.
Sample value metrics: 
% of capacity spent on top strategic priorities 
Reduced manual effort 
Faster cycle times 
Backlog burn down of high-value initiatives 
Time-to-value

The key upgrade is to translate outputs into outcomes.  

Cost 
You’ve already identified cost volatility, capacity constraints, and growing demand beyond capability. 
Sample cost metrics: 
Run v change ratio
External vs internal spend mix 
Cost per unit of output

The key upgrade is to translate cost per output to cost per outcome. 

Risk 
You already have a strong risk segment, including the following risk metrics: 
Cyber posture 
Patch compliance
System uptime 

The upgrade is to focus on the biggest source of risk - e.g., “a small number of complex programs account for most execution risk” 


Most importantly, you need to connect the KPIs to and highlight executive decisions/choices/tradeoffs - in other words, focusing on the “so what?” and “now what?”. Some relevant examples from your dashboard: 

Demand greater than capacity:
Choices:
- Stop low-value work
-Increase capacity
-Reprioritize portfolio
 Cost volatility:
Choices: 
-Shift sourcing model
-Prioritize ROI-positive initiatives only 
Complex Programs 
Choices: 
-Increase governance
-De-risk or phase delivery 

When it comes to benefits realization, you need to visualize a value chain that connects IT outputs to operational impact to business outcome. Ensure Benefit Realization After Initiative Delivery and Engage Business Stakeholders for Effective Benefits Realization

Overall, you can simplify the metrics for your CEO consumption through a one-page executive dashboard: See IT Dashboard for non-IT Executives.

Date: 15-Apr-26
Reference Number: 19433760
Buyer Region: NORTHAM
Buyer Industry: Manufacturing
Buyer Role: IT Sourcing / Procure / Vendor Mgmt - Other Role
Purpose: Observability Strategy Development
Question Asked: There is an active effort to define the observability strategy, including: - Evaluating whether to use a single tool or multiple tools for different environments (servers, applications, etc.). - Deciding between vendor-provided tools and internally developed solutions. - Assessing existing tools in the environment and determining criteria for retention or replacement.
The project is in the early stages, with a goal to finalize the plan and execution approach within the next couple of months.
How should we look at the tooling from an observability perspective? Should we be looking for one tool over the entire environment, or should there be multiple tools for servers, applications, etc.?
Should we be thinking about vendors bringing tools, or should we only buy our own tools and use those?
What criteria should we use to assess which existing tools to keep and which to retire?
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: Sent to the client:

Standardize on a single observability platform: While it is often necessary to retain multiple traditional monitoring tools, I recommend consolidating on a single observability platform as the primary system of insight. This platform should ingest diverse telemetry data, correlate signals across domains, and surface actionable, AI‑driven insights with minimal manual analysis. Establishing this foundation enables deeper value from ServiceNow, including future agentic AI and automated remediation capabilities.
Position ServiceNow ITOM as the central event correlation layer: Rather than attempting to directly integrate network or infrastructure monitoring tools into the observability platform, correlate and normalize those signals upstream within ServiceNow ITOM Event Management, where event aggregation and enrichment already occur.
Avoid duplicating event management functionality: Your decision to pass on tools like Splunk ITSI is well founded, as they primarily function as event correlation platforms and would duplicate capabilities already being implemented within ServiceNow ITOM.
Use the observability platform for SLI and SLO generation: Leverage the observability platform to derive custom metrics and calculate SLIs and SLOs close to the data source, then forward those results into ServiceNow to support service‑level visibility, reporting, and automation.
Anchor agentic AI within ITSM: Since incidents are created, triaged, and resolved in ITSM, I recommend beginning the agentic AI journey in ServiceNow. In this model, AI operates like an engineer that starts with the ticket and reaches back into observability tools for data, context, and validation.

- Cameron shared a self-created analysis matrix and requested Thomas C Lintemuth’s validation and expert insights on tool selection.
- Thomas confirmed familiarity with the matrix and agreed with most of Cameron’s analysis, particularly regarding tool capabilities.
- Thomas recommended considering Tufin, FireMon, and AlgoSec, noting Skybox is no longer available.
- He emphasized the importance of historical firewall log data for accurate analysis of unused rules, recommending at least 12 months of logs.
- Thomas explained that both Tufin and FireMon can ingest historical logs to report on unused and overly permissive rules.
- He clarified that these tools are compatible with both Cisco and Palo Alto firewalls and regularly update to support new vendor features.
- Thomas noted Tufin is typically faster at integrating new capabilities, while FireMon offers broader firewall support and is often more aggressively priced.
- He advised that running a report is quick, but the real challenge lies in identifying system owners and justifying rule changes to the business.
- Thomas recommended quarterly reviews of firewall rules, including implementing expiration dates and reauthorization processes for better hygiene.
- He explained that while automation for rule expiration is limited, integration with change management systems like ServiceNow can streamline processes.
- Thomas advised against one-off scans, recommending ongoing subscriptions due to the value of regular reviews, and estimated costs are moderate for three firewalls.
- For a single tool, Thomas gave a slight preference to Tufin, specifically its SecureTrack module, but noted AlgoSec’s Firewall Analyzer is also suitable.

Date: 24-Jun-26
Reference Number: 20149205
Buyer Region: EMEA
Buyer Industry: Government
Buyer Role: Divisional Technology Leader
Purpose: Automating SLA Tracking and Observability Across Hybrid Environments
Question Asked: We are currently experiencing challenges with managing SLAs across our environment. At present, SLA tracking is largely manual across our SaaS, cloud, and managed services.

We are looking for a solution that can help us automatically monitor and track SLAs, as well as provide visibility into changes across our infrastructure, applications, and cloud environment. We need to know where are the usage increasing and when are additional users added into our systems.
 
Questions:
Can Gartner recommend any tools?
How can we automate SLA tracking?
Analyst Name: Tom Cipolla
Discussion Summary: Dear Noura Al Sulaimani:

Thank you for your inquiry on SLA tracking.

Organizations trying to improve SLA tracking across SaaS, cloud, and managed services should expect to use a combination of tools rather than look for a single solution. SaaS management platforms (SMPs) such as Zylo, Torii, and Flexera are especially helpful for building visibility into the SaaS environment. They give you a clear view of who is using which applications, how license counts are changing, and when new users or applications are introduced. While SMPs don’t directly measure SLA performance—like uptime or response time—they provide important context, such as usage growth or contract terms, that can signal where SLA risks may emerge. In that sense, they act as a foundation for understanding SaaS consumption and change over time.
To actually monitor whether services are meeting SLA commitments, observability platforms like Datadog, Dynatrace, and New Relic are more directly aligned. These tools collect real-time performance and availability data across applications and infrastructure, allowing you to define service-level objectives and automatically detect when thresholds are breached. For SaaS applications, visibility can be more limited, but capabilities like synthetic monitoring and integrations with vendor status pages can still provide a useful proxy for availability and performance tracking.
ITSM platforms such as ServiceNow, BMC Helix, and Ivanti Neurons bring these insights together into an operational process. They allow you to define SLAs formally, track compliance, and automate how incidents and escalations are handled. When integrated with observability tools, they can automatically convert SLA breaches into tickets and workflows. Adding SMP data into this ecosystem provides additional context, such as which users or business units are affected and how vendor contracts align to the issue.
In practice, the most effective approach is to connect these capabilities. Observability tools track SLA performance in real time, ITSM platforms manage the workflows and accountability, and SMPs add visibility into SaaS usage and change. Together, they create a more complete and automated view of SLA management across the environment.
Recommended actions:
Integrate observability tools with ITSM to automate SLA monitoring and response
Use an SMP to establish visibility into SaaS usage, users, and contracts
Define consistent service-level objectives across all service types
Connect systems via APIs to share data and improve automation
Build a unified dashboard that combines SLA performance, usage trends, and incidents

- Sandeep explained their approach of attributing a percentage of overall business savings to APIs, but questioned its validity.
- Shrey Pasricha acknowledged the difficulty, noting APIs are often seen as backend plumbing, making direct value attribution complex.
- Shrey clarified there is no strict industry standard for API ROI, but recommended using a framework to justify integration value.
- Shrey reviewed Sandeep’s granular scorecard and asked about the methodology behind business enablement figures.
- Sandeep described allocating a portion of total business benefit to APIs, using a recent payment link implementation as an example.
- Shrey agreed this approach is reasonable, emphasizing that API value is typically a fraction of the enabled business outcome.
- Shrey recommended focusing on KPIs aligned with high-level business goals, such as revenue growth, cost reduction, or operational efficiency.
- He advised working backward from business objectives to identify which APIs enable those goals and deriving relevant KPIs.
- Shrey shared examples from other organizations, highlighting both operational metrics (e.g., active APIs) and business metrics (e.g., commerce driven).
- He stressed the importance of indirect measures, like customer retention or convenience, when APIs are not directly monetized.
- Shrey offered to share a comprehensive KPI spreadsheet and research to help Sandeep’s team refine their approach.
- He reiterated there is no universal format, and organizations should tailor metrics to their context, involving stakeholders for input.
- The call concluded with Shrey committing to send supporting materials and Sandeep planning to integrate these insights into their dashboard.

What is the overall outlook of vendors providing their solutions on-premise. Are on-premise offerings going away in favor of cloud/saas by the vendors? Are there any predictions, st
Analyst Name: Ted McHugh
Discussion Summary: 1.	How are organizations who need high levels of security using cloud placement. For example, US DoD or other top secret agencies in other organizations. What are their placement strategies? Are they putting their workloads in cloud? Are they creating sovereign clouds? Or keeping the on-prem. What do they do when it comes to SaaS which can have confidential data? Do you have any studies around this topics that covers agencies from across the regions not just the US.
This varies from country to country and even agency to agency. A lot will still avoid public cloud for workloads classified secret or above – and retain them in their own private cloud, or shared cloud with other government agencies. We see this regularly in Europe for example, due to concerns around the US Cloud Act or other sovereignty risks. For less sensitive workloads, they will often be deployed to a normal or perhaps sovereign cloud region from one of the US hyperscalers.  Sometimes – but not often, we encounter distributed cloud being used for sensitive workloads such as AWS Outposts, Azure Local, OCI Isolated Region or GCP Distributed Compute. The air-gapped offerings from Azure, GCP and OCI are also gaining a lot of attention – but these solutions tend to be much more expensive, while still lacking some key benefits of the public cloud. It’s worth highlighting that the level of security even in the mainstream public cloud will generally be higher than what most organizations can built themselves – if configured correctly. I rarely see European (or other non-US) cloud providers being used for government workloads although this may increase in the coming years as the US Partner Clouds (S3NS/GCP and Blue/Azure) become more mainstream, or local providers start to win local gov cloud type contracts. 

In the US, the different Gov Cloud options (AWS GovCloud, Azure GCC & GCC High, etc.) are commonly utilized by all types of government agencies. For higher secrecy workloads, AWS (Secret/Top Secret), Azure (Secret/Top Secret)  and Oracle(National Security Region) also offer physically and logically isolated options. And still, it is common to encounter US Gov Agencies with a significant on-premise footprint and little to no cloud footprint – although many are struggling to justify the high cost of refresh or replacement Vs moving to the cloud. There also appears to be a significant cost and operational overhead when using GCC High and above, which is driving some agencies to be very selective with their workload placement, only using these options when really needed, very much treating it as a Multicloud environment. 

It is rare to see SaaS being used for highly confidential data, and the critically and data classification are two key primary drivers around the use of SaaS versus IaaS or PaaS. Obviously solutions like MS365 and Google Workspace are used heavily in Europe, but there has been a distinct push to move to alternative platforms by many EU countries. Most are planning to leverage opensource components, with some custom integrations as no fully functional, fully integrated alternatives exist. In the US, some major vendors such as MS, ServiceNow and Salesforce have government options, which I believe are logically isolated instances of their platforms specifically for government agencies. I have not encountered this model outside of the US, likely for similar sovereignty reasons as the use of public cloud.

Purpose: Efficient System Monitoring Migration
Question Asked: Previously, our organization relied on ATOS to provide essential IT tools, including system monitoring solutions. Currently, ATOS supplies us with ServiceNow, which we continue to use, but have found increasingly expensive. For system monitoring, we have adopted NetGain, a less common tool chosen to minimize migration complexity since it aligns with ATOS’s existing setup. Our monitoring environment is extensive, with over 30,000 rules applied across various devices, each with unique thresholds and notification procedures. Migrating to a new monitoring platform would require manually recreating these rules a resource-intensive and time-consuming process. We have tested PRTG as a potential alternative, confirming it can replicate the capabilities of our current ATOS platform. However, limited resources and time constraints have hindered a full migration. After negotiations, ATOS has agreed to sell us the NetGain platform and provide the configuration database.
Analyst Name: D.B. Cummings
Discussion Summary: This is the Written Response emailed to the client:

Dear Timothy Lee:

As I understand your situation, Dah Sing Bank is transitioning from a vendor-managed monitoring model toward internal ownership and support. You want to preserve your existing monitoring coverage while reducing operational overhead. The guidance below addresses your questions directly, focusing on process, structure, and execution considerations. 

Introduction

Treat your transition from the ATOS‑managed NetGain environment to a fully self‑managed monitoring platform as a strategic transformation and not just a simple tooling change. With more than 30,000 monitoring configurations in scope, you must deliberately plan the migration to avoid carrying legacy complexity and alert noise into the new environment. Use this transition to regain operational control, transparency, and long‑term independence, while explicitly preparing for the added responsibilities that come with internal ownership.

Approach this effort as both a technical and an operational redesign. Do not default to recreating the existing environment rule‑for‑rule. Instead, use the migration to modernize how monitoring supports business outcomes and operational clarity.

You asked “What best practices should we follow when transitioning from vendor-managed IT tools to self-managed solutions, particularly for monitoring systems?”

Avoid a mechanical lift‑and‑shift of existing configurations. Begin by clearly defining what you want monitoring to achieve in the new environment, such as improving availability, resilience, and user experience rather than simply reproducing device health metrics. Establish success criteria early so design decisions remain aligned with business and operational priorities.

Inventory the existing rule set and rationalize it. Identify stale, redundant, and low‑value alerts, and eliminate them rather than migrating them. Use the transition as an opportunity to reduce alert fatigue and improve signal quality. Where feasible, shift from static, component‑level thresholds toward service‑oriented indicators that reflect the health of business‑critical services instead of individual devices.

Standardize monitoring design wherever possible. Use normalized data models, reusable templates, and consistent patterns to reduce customization overhead. Design the new monitoring environment to be simpler to operate and maintain once ownership transfers fully to internal teams.

You asked, “Are there automated methods or tools available to facilitate the migration of complex monitoring rules and configurations between platforms such as NetGain and PRTG?”

You will not be able to manually recreate the monitoring configurations at this scale. At the same time, I am not aware of any vendor-provided or out-of-the-box tools that support a direct migration from NetGain to PRTG. Migrations of this type are typically handled through custom export and transformation approaches rather than packaged tooling.

One potential approach is to treat the migration as a data extraction and transformation exercise. Once the NetGain configuration database is available, configuration elements such as rule definitions, thresholds, and notification logic might be able to be extracted programmatically, depending on how the data is structured and accessible. From there, scripting tools such as Python could be used to normalize and map these configurations into the target platform’s object model.

For PRTG, this would involve translating monitoring concepts into devices, sensors, and alerting constructs rather than expecting a direct one-to-one rule conversion. This is a significant consideration because NetGain’s rule-based monitoring model does not directly align with PRTG’s device-and-sensor-based architecture. As a result, a one-to-one mapping of existing rules is not feasible and may lead to a substantial increase in the number of

Discussion Summary: Key Takeaways:

 

GRC is something of a “meta-market” in the sense that it is actually several, partially distinct but interrelated markets of tools. Our overall view of this market is contained in the “Magic Quadrant” below.
The core use cases of that “meta-market” align with your “ERM use cases” from the slides that you attached. Most or all of the tools in the market have workflows designed to accomplish those things.
… However, the devil is in the details. Risk management functions and audit work around defined frameworks and policies, so they’re very sensitive to having tool workflows that exactly match their specified processes. Therefore, robust requirements documentation and process discovery is key. I recommend the “RFP Toolkit” below as a resource for this.
The GRC vendors – especially “enterprise” GRC vendors (like ServiceNow. See last two resources below on “enterprise” and other types of GRC vendors.) – often market that data integration can only be assured if customers have all of their users on the vendors’ modules/solutions. However, data connectors, APIs, etc. call this into question. Moreover, due to the point directly above, you often won’t get the data to integrate in the first place with tool selection that doesn’t match users’ workflow needs.

Analyst Name: Kelli Smith
Discussion Summary: Hi Jane,

I received your request for a written response inquiry, relating to geographic expansion to the Middle East, specifically the UAE and Saudi Arabia—there are a few consistent patterns worth highlighting.
GTM model (Direct vs. Indirect):
Across the region, most established LCAP vendors operate a hybrid go‑to‑market model, combining direct sales with a strong partner‑led motion.
•	Vendors typically maintain local or regional sales offices to directly engage large enterprises and government entities. Direct sales is most common for complex deals and strategic accounts.
•	At the same time, partners (GSIs, regional SIs, and local consultancies) play a critical role where local presence, delivery capacity, and regulatory familiarity are essential. Indirect routes are heavily used for implementation, customization, and scaling into additional accounts once demand is established.
•	In mid‑market scenarios, some LCAP vendors may skew to be a bit more partner‑led overall but still retain direct coverage for key opportunities and verticals.
Use cases used to penetrate the market:
From an offering perspective, LCAP vendors typically lead with business‑outcome‑driven use cases rather than “platform” positioning. The main entry point in both UAE and Saudi Arabia is application modernization, including:
•	Replacing legacy workflow and case management systems
•	Digitizing manual or paper‑based processes
•	Improving operational efficiency and service delivery (especially in government, financial services, oil & gas, and regulated industries)
Other types of use cases include:
•	Process automation and orchestration (often tied to efficiency and cost‑containment mandates)
•	Case management and citizen experience modernization
•	Compliance‑driven workflow digitization
LCAP vendors with strong market share in this region include Salesforce, ServiceNow, Microsoft, Appian, and Outsystems. Please see Market Share: Enterprise Software, Worldwide, 2025 and filter by the market and region. (I am also happy to walk you through this in an inquiry.) 

I’ve outlined recommended research below:
Forecast Analysis: Low-Code Development Technologies, Worldwide 

Forecast Analysis: Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies, Worldwide
